items.title: Explainer-What are the disputes between Iraq's federal government and Kurdistan region?
items.content:
Nov 24 (Reuters) - Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi on Tuesday ordered federal authorities to take over border crossings in the semi-autonomous Kurdistan region and directed the oil ministry to manage oilfields under Kurdish security control in four provinces, following an oil smuggling investigation at the state-run North Oil Company.
The orders are part of a broader crackdown byZaidi against oil smuggling. They also reopen long-running disputes between Baghdad and the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) overcontrol of oil, money, territory and trade.

Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, despite concerns over his conduct and the supply of AI chips to China, may show that AI – and Huang himself – are ‘too big to fail’.

items.title: Saudi finance minister claims kingdom can withstand prolonged Houthi conflict
items.content:
Saudi finance minister claims kingdom can withstand prolonged Houthi conflict
Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed al-Jadaan says the kingdom is “resilient enough to withstand a prolonged conflict” with Yemen’s Houthis.
Speaking to reporters, al-Jadaan dismissed as “a total mistake” any expectation that attacks on civilian infrastructure or “blackmail by missiles” would force Riyadh to compromise its national security.
He said Saudi Arabia plans to reduce its budget deficit to 3.6 percent of GDP in 2027, compared with an estimated 4.9 percent this year, despite the escalating fighting.
The Iran-backed Houthis say their missile and drone campaign aims to force Riyadh to withdraw support for Yemen’s government.
Al-Jadaan said reduced oil production had driven a 2.1 percent contraction in Saudi GDP this year.

items.title: Between hope and grief, Palestinian families wait for sons' bodies
items.content:
Palestinian construction worker Wael Sheghnoubi has been waiting in vain for his son Nidal's body since he was killed by the Israeli military in May 2025, unable to move on.
"When someone buries a martyr it brings relief. They haven't given us anything," said Sheghnoubi, holding a photo of his 16-year-old son in his home in the West Bank village of Burqa.
Israel's military frequently retains bodies of Palestinians, whether they are armed militants in Gaza or teens throwing rocks in the occupied West Bank.

items.title: 'Political theatre': Campaigners hit out at EU hypocrisy as Cop31 ends in chaos
items.content:
'Political theatre': Campaigners hit out at EU hypocrisy as Cop31 ends in chaos
Submitted by
Katherine Hearst
on
Tue, 11/24/2026 - 13:44
Developing countries say they felt kept in the dark and were not consulted during the drafting of the final text
Australian Minister for Climate Change and Energy and President of Cop31 Negotiations Chris Bowen at a plenary session at the UN Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Turkey, 22 November 2026 (Reuters)
Off
On Sunday, fraught global climate talks in
Turkey
, the longest ever in the climate conference’s history, ground to a halt, with
no deal
. The EU,
UK
and allies rejected the draft text over its failure to mention fossil fuels.
At the closing plenary, Ireland’s Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien, on behalf of the EU, rejected the text, saying it “does not respond to the science, and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required… that does not even mention fossil fuels”.
His words were met with applause. But they rang hollow for developing countries, many of whom also rejected the text over its weak language on climate finance.
After delivering his intervention, O’Brien and EU Climate Minister Wopke Hoekstra
walked out of the plenary to hold a press huddle
while developing nations were speaking about the need for climate finance.
While the EU, UK and allies cited the omission of fossil fuels from the text as their main reason for rejecting it, climate justice campaigners
reported
that developed countries and EU officials had spent the duration of the talks blocking measures which would require them to make fresh finance commitments.
“The EU used fossil fuels as the main reason for their rejection of the text. But the other issue, or what I would call the most important issue, is climate finance,” Harjeet Singh, strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative and the global convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign, told Middle East Eye.
“If you listened to what other countries said, like Panama, Ghana, the Marshall Islands, their reasons were no money for adaptation, no money for loss and damage.”
Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, developed countries are
required
to provide finance to help developing countries cut emissions and adapt to climate impacts.
According to the UN’s
latest report
, published earlier this month, developing countries will need about $300bn annually in adaptation funding by 2035.
At Cop26 in 2021, developed countries agreed to at least double adaptation finance by 2025, with 2019 levels, $19bn, as a benchmark.
Last year, they agreed to a call to “at least triple” adaptation finance by 2035. But the final text left ambiguities around the baseline year.
An earlier draft of this year’s text, released on 16 November, stipulated a target annual figure of at least $120bn, with a baseline of $40bn a year.
But the sums were quietly dropped from subsequent drafts. Climate justice campaigners laid the blame for this squarely at the doors of the EU and wealthier countries who they
say
"came with nothing" and thwarted progress on discussions around climate finance.
During this year’s “Contributor Dialogue” at the conference, which aimed to fill the starved fund, a handful of developed countries pledged just $30m, significantly down from last year’s sum of $120m.
“So we have a fund that no one wants to fill,” Singh said.
Dead in the water
Even before the summit had started, Hoekstra set the tone for negotiations by proclaiming climate finance “dead in the water”.
“They entered negotiations with that bad faith and blocked every single track which is important for developing countries,” Singh told MEE.
According to
Climate Action Network,
the EU and other developed countries refused to engage on a baseline for tripling adaptation finance.
Cop31 draft agreement ‘the worst ever', campaigners warn
Read More »
“We agreed on the baseline, I was witness to that process in 2019,” Singh said.
“So they just want to create new processes and new loops so that we can just continue talking.”
Singh also pointed to what he described as the hypocrisy of the EU and wealthy countries’ stance on fossil fuel language in the draft text.
"Norway and Ireland, who were arguing for the inclusion of fossil fuel language in the text, are back home expanding fossil fuel production,” he said.
The EU’s own “roadmaps” for transitions away from fossil fuels have drawn criticism for
restating existing policies
that are not aligned with the 1.5 degree temperature goal.
Brandon Wu, director of policy and campaigns at Action Aid USA,
slammed
the EU’s transition plans as a “smokescreen”.
“They’re using the rhetoric around fossil fuels to make themselves look like champions," Wu told reporters.
For Singh, a Cop veteran who has attended the last 18 conferences, the EU’s actions are tantamount to little more than “political theatre”.
“Do your work. We need to move beyond these theatrics and take real action, rather than simply claiming leadership. Be a real leader. Provide the money. Take action at home in line with your fair share of the global effort,” he said.
‘Extremely disrespected’
Campaigners told Middle East Eye that the talks’ meltdown was also due in part to the weak and untransparent facilitation by the joint presidents, Australia and Turkey.
“There was no stocktaking plenary where countries could share their opinion, where things could be dragged out in the open. When they said they would publish text, they didn’t do so,” Andreas Sieber, associate director of global policy at 350.org, told MEE.
'Norway and Ireland, who were arguing for the inclusion of fossil fuel language in the text, are back home expanding fossil fuel production'
- Harjeet Singh, strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative
MEE understands that many developing countries felt they were left in the dark and not consulted while the text was being drafted.
Cop presidents usually release printed versions of drafts for parties to review. But this year, only selected groups were shown excerpts, leaving many developing countries feeling “extremely disrespected and extremely badly treated,” one observer said.
Hanen Keskes of Greenpeace Mena said that the process of revising the second draft of the Cop text was very unclear.
“From what I've heard from parties, they had not been consulted,” Keskes told MEE. “It was very unclear what progress happened between the 19th and 22nd on other agenda items that were quite important.
“When the new text came out on Saturday night, it was essentially the same text from the 19th. So clearly no consultation had been done.”
The acrimony was summed up in a searing rebuke of the Cop presidency by Ghana’s Environment Minister Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, who was “rudely cut off” during her delivery by Murat Kurum, Cop31 president and Turkey's environment minister.
“This excellency is an example of the levels of disrespect we have endured and continue to express our objection to. It absolutely does not respect multilateralism,” she said.

items.title: Yemen ministry puts losses from Saudi attacks and blockade above $1.13 trillion
items.content:
Yemen ministry puts losses from Saudi attacks and blockade above $1.13 trillion
Yemen’s Houthi-run Economy Ministry says Saudi attacks and the blockade have inflicted more than $1.13 trillion in cumulative economic losses since the war began began in March 2015.
Acting Economy Minister Sam al-Bashiri said preliminary estimates put direct damage during the latest escalation, from 13 July to 23 November, at more than $881.5m, Saba reports.
He said Saudi strikes destroyed 22 factories and partially damaged three others, causing industrial losses exceeding $376m.
The ministry put commercial losses above $85m and investment-sector losses above $20m.
Transport and Public Works Minister Mohammed Quhaim reported more than $350m in damage to infrastructure and other sectors during the same period.
Quhaim said attacks on airports, ports, roads and bridges had disrupted supplies and increased shipping, insurance and storage costs, placing further financial pressure on Yemenis.
The announcement provided no detailed methodology for the cumulative trillion-dollar estimate.

items.title: Ahmad Tibi ‘most threatened’ MP in Israel amid rising anti-Palestinian incitement
items.content:
Ahmad Tibi ‘most threatened’ MP in Israel amid rising anti-Palestinian incitement
Submitted by
Nadav Rapaport
on
Tue, 11/24/2026 - 13:52
Knesset security chief tells Palestinian lawmaker to ‘take care of himself and be careful’
Ahmad Tibi, head of the Arab Movement for Change (Ta'al) party, speaks during an interview with AFP in the northern Israeli city of Nazareth on 2 November 2026 (Ahmad Gharabli/AFP)
Off
Palestinian lawmaker and Israeli citizen Ahmad Tibi is the most "threatened" member of Israel's parliament, according to the Knesset's security chief.
Israel Hayom
reported
on Monday that Tibi, a member of the Palestinian-led Joint List alliance, had been told to "take care of himself and be careful" by Yuval Chen, commander of the Knesset Guard, the security unit responsible for protecting Israel's parliament.
Chen reportedly told Tibi that he was “the most threatened member of the Knesset”.
Sources in the Joint List accused the Knesset Guard of failing to provide adequate protection for Palestinian lawmakers inside the Knesset.
"Where are the Knesset Guard officers when they are needed? Why aren't they stationed permanently at the door of the Joint List during parliamentary group meetings?" they told the Israeli newspaper.
The warning to Tibi follows an incident on Monday in which Israeli comedian and right-wing figure Guy Hochman put his arms around the lawmaker while attempting to film a video.
Tibi pushed Hochman away after the comedian entered his personal space, prompting accusations that the Palestinian MP had assaulted him.
Hochman filed a complaint against Tibi with the Knesset Guard, alleging that the lawmaker had assaulted him. Ma'ariv also
reported
that a complaint against Tibi had been submitted to Israel's attorney general, Gali Baharav-Miara.
Why Palestinian electoral gains in Israel cannot alter the racist structure of the state
Ghada Majadli
Read More »
Tibi, however, said he felt threatened when Hochman invaded his personal space on Knesset premises and that he had acted in self-defence.
"Hochman is a bad actor. He suddenly shoved a phone in my face, I pushed the phone away, and since then I've been told he went into intensive care," Tibi told Ma'ariv.
Tibi said he had also filed a complaint against Hochman with the Knesset Guard, saying he had "felt threatened".
In a letter to the security unit, Tibi said Hochman had "approached me from behind, grabbed me without my consent, and shoved a phone to my face in an invasive and threatening manner".
"The incident is especially serious against the backdrop of the threats, incitement, and smears directed at me since the elections," the letter said.
It referred to the growing incitement against Tibi by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies since the Joint List and Ra'am won a historic 19 seats in the Knesset in last month's elections.
Anti-Palestinian incitement
Tibi also accused the Knesset Guard of discriminating against Palestinian lawmakers.
"It is highly doubtful that an Arab man who behaved this way towards a Jewish minister would have received similar treatment, without the immediate intervention of the guards, who would have slammed him to the ground," he said.
"The security and dignity of Arab Knesset Members are not fair game," Tibi added, demanding an investigation into the incident.
Meanwhile, far-right Israeli politicians used the confrontation to launch fresh attacks against the Palestinian lawmaker.
Israeli MP invokes internment of Japanese Americans in call to restrict Palestinian citizens
Read More »
Outgoing Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich urged Jewish opposition parties, led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, not to form a government dependent on votes from the Joint List and Ra'am.
"This is what happens when they feel like the masters of the land; parliamentary violence turns into physical violence," Smotrich
said
, accusing Tibi of assaulting Hochman.
"The police must immediately open a criminal investigation against Ahmad Tibi," the settler leader added on X.
Two MPs from the party of outgoing National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir, Otzma Yehudit, also attacked Tibi.
On Monday, Tally Gotliv
stormed
a Joint List parliamentary group meeting, while Hanamel Dorfman
wrote
on X: "The doctor of terror is also a doctor of violence."
Tibi is a qualified gynaecologist.
Tibi, who was elected last week as one of the Knesset's deputy speakers, has become a prominent target of the far-right incitement campaign against Palestinians in Israel since the elections.
He is not the only Palestinian to face such hostility.
Last week, a mosque in the village of Ed-Dahi was set on fire in a suspected
arson attack
linked to an Israeli mob.

items.title: UK invokes ‘British values’ in latest Houthi sanctions, makes no mention of ally Saudi Arabia
items.content:
UK invokes ‘British values’ in latest Houthi sanctions, makes no mention of ally Saudi Arabia
Britain has imposed fresh sanctions on Yemen’s Houthis, accusing the group of “serious human rights abuses” and efforts to “undermine” Middle Eastern stability.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband linked the measures to attacks on merchant vessels in Bab al-Mandeb, saying they had “driven up the cost of living at home”.
He said the sanctions sent a “clear message” that Britain would “act in support of British values and interests,” according to a government statement.
“The Houthis’ renewed aggression targeting our partners and innocent civilians is unacceptable, and they must be held to account,” said Miliband.
The British government made no mention of its ally Saudi Arabia, which it is helping in an advisory role and with military hardware to carry out attacks on Yemen that have killed hundreds of civilians.

items.title: Rohingya genocide case: How The Gambia went to The Hague and won
items.content:
Rohingya genocide case: How The Gambia went to The Hague and won
Submitted by
Sondos Asem
on
Sun, 11/22/2026 - 15:04
Lead counsel Arsalan Suleman tells Middle East Eye how the small African country took Myanmar to court and how survivor testimony helped secure a landmark judgement
Eighty years after the International Court of Justice (ICJ) first sat in The Hague, I walked into the Peace Palace’s Great Hall of Justice to photograph the judges as they took their seats.
They were about to deliver
a landmark judgment
in a trailblazing case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar. For the first time, the court would find that a state had committed genocide, the "
crime of all crimes
" as it has been described.
It had been seven years since The Gambia, a slither of a country of less than three million people in West Africa that is named after the river that dissects it, filed the case.
It argued that Myanmar was trying to destroy the Rohingya, a predominantly Muslim minority that has lived in Rakhine State on the country's western coast for generations.
The case was brought under the
1948 Genocide Convention
, the UN’s first human rights treaty, drawn up in the wake of the Holocaust to define genocide under international law and require states to prevent and punish it.
In the past, international criminal tribunals have convicted individuals of genocide, such as in courts created to prosecute atrocities committed during the wars in the former Yugoslavia and in Rwanda in the 1990s.
But this time the question before the ICJ, the UN’s highest court which adjudicates mainly in disputes between states, was whether Myanmar itself, as a state actor, can be held responsible.
In 2017, Myanmar’s military
burned Rohingya villages
, carried out mass killings and widespread rape, and deliberately killed children, the court found. Soldiers shot civilians as they fled, including people trying to swim to safety.
More than 700,000 fled to neighbouring Bangladesh, which now houses the world’s largest refugee camp in
Cox’s Bazar
, hosting over one million Rohingya refugees.
(L-R) Paul Reichler, Arsalan Suleman and Gambian Justice Minister Dawda Jallow await the final judgment at the ICJ on 19 November 2026 (MEE)
Some of the survivors and witnesses were already sobbing as they entered the hall.
Arsalan Suleman, the
American
lawyer who helped The Gambia bring the case and led its legal team, looked composed and greeted me with a confident smile.
The previous day, the court’s press team had shown journalists the two rooms the judges use before entering the courtroom.
In the Green Room, where they put on their black robes and white lace collars, a namecard stood on the table in front of each chair.
The judges then gather in the Red Room, beneath portraits of former court presidents. The press team also showed us the seating plan, so I knew Navi Pillay, the South African judge last month
awarded
the Nobel Peace Prize, would be the first judge through the door.
I was struck by how many reporters had turned up. The press room was full, so the court streamed the proceedings in its cafeteria. I had 10 minutes inside the courtroom to photograph the opening.
'La Cour!'
As we waited for the judges to enter, the room fell silent.
I turned my camera towards the judges’ entrance. Along the wood-panelled hall, four stained-glass windows by the Scottish artist Douglas Strachan depict war in reds and purples and a future at peace in blues and whites.
“La Cour!” the usher called, prompting those inside the courtroom to stand as he opened the door. Above him hung Peace through Justice, Albert Besnard’s painting depicting a goddess of peace standing between two warring parties.
Pillay came through first, followed by the other 14 judges who make up the ICJ's bench, each of them to serve nine-year terms by UN member states.
The Gambia had chosen Pillay, a former UN human rights chief, to sit as an ad hoc judge in the case.
Pillay was
awarded
the Nobel Peace Prize for her work promoting peace and international law. Hours after the prize was announced on 9 October, the US
announced sanctions
against the International Criminal Court, where Pillay was one of the first judges.
Navi Pillay enters the ICJ courtroom, 19 November 2026 (Reuters)
Also based in The Hague, the ICC prosecutes individuals for crimes including genocide.
Weeks before the Rohingya judgment,
Mike Waltz
, the US ambassador to the UN, had accused Pillay of trying to lower the threshold for proving genocide in order to target Americans and their allies, and warned that Washington would be "watching" the proceedings closely. But Pillay appeared defiant as she led the judges into the hall.
At the UN’s International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, the ad hoc court she also previously led, Pillay was one of three judges who
convicted
former Rwandan mayor Jean-Paul Akayesu in 1998.
It was the first time an international court found an individual guilty of genocide. Pillay led the drafting of the part of the judgment that established that rape and other forms of sexual violence can constitute acts of genocide, also a first under international law.
Most recently, she had chaired the UN’s independent commission of inquiry on occupied
Palestine
and
Israel
, which concluded last year that Israel had committed
genocide
against Palestinians in Gaza.
On 19 November, with Pillay in the nine-to-six majority, the ICJ ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in northern Rakhine State during its military’s horrific attacks on the group nine years earlier.
'We are very happy'
After the judgement, Suleman celebrated with Rohingya survivors and his colleagues, a silver garland around his neck. Others wore blue, golden, and silver garlands, in keeping with a Rohingya celebratory custom.
“We are very happy that finally we got a positive verdict, and we’ve got almost all of what we asked the court to deliver,” Dawda Jallow, The Gambia’s justice minister and its representative before the court, told Middle East Eye. “This is unprecedented.”
The following day, at Suleman’s hotel a few minutes’ walk away from the Peace Palace, we spoke for an hour about how this extraordinary and unprecedented case came together - and the long and winding path to justice as circuitous as the Gambia river itself.
The Gambia team and Rohingya survivors celebrate after the ICJ delivered the genocide judgement (MEE)
Suleman is a Muslim American of Pakistani heritage, born and raised in New Orleans. He studied international security at Georgetown University’s School of Foreign Service, before earning a master’s degree in international peace studies from Trinity College Dublin and then as law degree from Harvard Law School.
Now a partner at the US law firm Foley Hoag, he previously served under President Barack Obama as acting US special envoy to
the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC)
, a group of 57 countries with its headquarters in
Saudi Arabia
that promotes cooperation among its members and aims to represent the interests of the world's Muslim-majority nations.
The relationships he built there helped him bring the idea for a case to The Gambia.
From Bangladesh to The Hague
The case put mainland Africa’s smallest country, a Muslim-majority democracy on the Atlantic coast, at the centre of a landmark ruling on genocide.
The Gambia already has pedigree in the field of international justice. Its capital, Banjul, hosts the secretariat of
the African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights
, and a former Gambian justice minister,
Fatou Bensouda
, went on to become chief prosecutor of the International Criminal Court.
The Gambia’s involvement in what would become the genocide case against Myanmar began in May 2018, when Bangladesh hosted a meeting of OIC foreign ministers in Dhaka.
The Rohingya crisis was on the agenda, including how to help the hundreds of thousands of refugees by then seeking safety in Bangladesh and hold those responsible for abuses in Myanmar to account.
The Gambia’s foreign minister was unable to attend the Dhaka meeting, Suleman said, so President Adama Barrow sent his justice minister, Abubacarr Tambadou, in his place. As part of the meeting, Bangladesh took delegates to the refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar, where Tambadou met Rohingya survivors.
Justice and accountability were already priorities at home. Gambians had voted out longtime ruler
Yahya Jammeh in 2016
to end 22 years of authoritarian rule plagued by human rights abuses.
It had also taken a brief
military intervention
by Senegal, Nigeria and Ghana through the Ecowas bloc of West African states to force Jammeh to step down.
Barrow’s new government had made truth and reconciliation part of its mandate.
Tambadou had spent almost nine years prosecuting genocide at the UN’s Rwanda tribunal.
“So when he met the victims, he knew what he was seeing,” Suleman explained.
Abubacarr Tambadou, then Minister of Justice of The Gambia (R) waves to a representative of the Rohingya community prior to an interim ICJ ruling on 23 January 2020 (AFP)
Tambadou worked with OIC officials to set up a committee on accountability, which The Gambia chaired.
Around the same time, Suleman and his colleagues at Foley Hoag were exploring whether a case could be brought under the Genocide Convention. When he raised the idea with former contacts at the OIC, one told him to speak to the Gambians.
Suleman met Tambadou in New York that September, during the UN General Assembly. Some early discussions had focused on international criminal tribunals, which prosecute individuals, Suleman recalled.
The ICJ offered a way to hold Myanmar itself responsible. Tambadou invited him to present the committee with legal options in Banjul, the Gambian capital, the following February.
The committee backed an ICJ case, and the OIC’s foreign ministers and heads of state endorsed it.
The Gambia’s president and cabinet then approved bringing the case. The government appointed Suleman and his firm and filed its application on 11 November 2019. Suleman went on to lead the legal team.
OIC members also helped pay for the case. In a
statement
issued after the judgment, the OIC Secretary-General Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed thanked a number of countries for their "generous financial contributions" including Saudi Arabia,
Turkey
, Malaysia, Bangladesh,
Kuwait
, Nigeria, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Afghanistan.
Military coup
The Gambia first asked the court for emergency measures to protect the Rohingya while the case proceeded.
In December 2019, Aung San Suu Kyi, Myanmar’s then civilian leader and herself a Nobel Peace Prize winner in 1991 during her long imprisonment by the military government, led the country’s delegation at the hearing.
The following month, the judges unanimously ordered Myanmar to take steps to prevent acts of genocide, preserve evidence and report on its compliance. The final judgment found that Myanmar breached the order to preserve evidence.
Myanmar challenged the court’s jurisdiction in January 2021, shortly before the military seized power from the elected civilian government.
The coup raised the question of who could speak for Myanmar. Suu Kyi could no longer represent the country, and both the military authorities and representatives of the ousted parliament claimed the right to do so.
Myanmar's then State Counsellor Aung San Suu Kyi (C) stands before the ICJ on 11 December 2019 (AFP)
Suleman said the dispute contributed to the delay. He said he understood why the years of waiting felt especially long to the Rohingya in the camps.
Myanmar argued that the OIC was the real applicant and that The Gambia had no right to bring the case. In July 2022, the court dismissed those objections.
The Gambia had filed in its own name. As a party to the Genocide Convention, it could hold another party to its obligations under the treaty. That right extended to countries whose own nationals had suffered no direct harm.
How the lawyers built the case
Earlier UN investigations gave Suleman and his team a starting point and provided some of the key evidence the court relied on.
In March 2017, the UN Human Rights Council set up an independent fact-finding mission to investigate alleged abuses by Myanmar’s military and security forces, particularly in Rakhine State.
The following year the council created another body known as the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM) with a different purpose: to collect, preserve and analyse evidence of serious international crimes and prepare case files for possible prosecutions.
The mission interviewed hundreds of Rohingya refugees and documented years of discrimination and hate speech, as well as mass killings, sexual violence and the destruction of villages.
The Rohingya case that could redefine the law on genocide
Read More »
Suleman described the mission’s 2018 report as “the anchor around which the case could be built”.
Investigators looked at what happened before and after the attacks.
Suleman described how troops went to villages in advance, forced residents to take down fences and confiscated items that could be used as weapons, including kitchen knives.
Investigators later used satellite data to document the destruction of villages. Burning them, Suleman said, destroyed evidence and made it harder for the Rohingya to return.
Most of the evidence went to the judges in written submissions running to hundreds of pages, backed by thousands more pages of documents. Those included statements from survivors gathered by organisations such as Legal Action Worldwide.
In the final judgment, the court found the fact-finding mission’s reports generally reliable, even though it used a lower standard of proof than the court.
Judges gave considerable weight to the IIMM’s detailed witness statements and reports because of its rigorous methods, and to satellite data that helped confirm accounts of villages being burned.
Witness statements collected by
Legal Action Worldwide
were also generally reliable, the judges found, though they carried less weight because they were less detailed. As Suleman explained, evidence given less weight could still help confirm another account.
At the January 2026 hearings, Suleman divided the arguments among the lawyers. Some covered the history of discrimination and the pattern of attacks. Others explained how the evidence, taken together, met the court’s standard for proving intent. Suleman’s oral intervention argued that the Myanmar military’s hate speech and propaganda helped show why the Rohingya were targeted.
The Gambia
called
a military expert, Michael Newton, to address Myanmar’s account of the operations.
It also called three Rohingya survivors, who testified in closed sessions about what happened in their villages. Members of the legal team prepared them for questions from the judges and the possibility of cross-examination.
What persuaded the judges
The court found three forms of genocidal conduct proved: killing, causing serious physical or psychological harm, and imposing measures intended to prevent births.
The judges found that Myanmar targeted about 815,000 Rohingya in northern Rakhine State. That is roughly 58 percent of the 1.4 million Rohingya that Myanmar said lived in the country at the time.
The court found that the group targeted was large enough to constitute a “substantial part” of the Rohingya population under the Genocide Convention.
The judges said the evidence supported the UN fact-finding mission’s estimate of at least 10,000 deaths. But that was not the only factor that explained the genocidal campaign. The scale of the attacks also had to account for people who suffered serious physical or psychological harm or were subjected to measures intended to prevent births.
'The Gambia simply asked that the court apply its standard to the facts that The Gambia presented, and that’s what the court did'
- Arsalan Suleman, The Gambia's lawyer
Meanwhile, Myanmar claimed that its forces had passed up opportunities to kill more Rohingya, but the court responded that a finding of genocidal intent did not depend on whether the military had done everything it could to destroy the group.
In
Min Gyi village
, soldiers separated and executed men, killed children and opened fire on people trying to flee across a river.
The court held that the military’s sexual violence primarily targeted women and girls of reproductive age, including pregnant women in some cases.
The judges cited evidence that girls as young as seven were raped. Witnesses described children being shot or killed in burning homes. People who tried to escape across a river came under fire from soldiers. Some, particularly children and older people, drowned.
The court’s finding that Myanmar took measures intended to prevent Rohingya births was based on restrictions on marriage and childbirth, the denial of birth registration to Rohingya children and the scale of the military’s sexual violence.
To provide genocidal intent, the ICJ applied the test it had used in earlier cases brought against Serbia by Croatia and Bosnia in relation to the conflicts in the former Yugoslavia.
The judges had to be fully convinced by the evidence that acts of genocide had occurred and that Myanmar’s forces intended to destroy the Rohingya, in whole or in part. Because the court was inferring intent from circumstantial evidence, genocidal intent had to be the only reasonable inference from the facts taken together.
Myanmar argued that its campaign against the Rohingya was a counter-insurgency operation, and that other motives that could explain its conduct included a desire to drive the Rohingya out or to punish the civilian population.
But the court rejected all these explanations and said the “only reasonable inference” to be drawn from Myanmar’s conduct was genocide.
“The Gambia did not ask for any change in the standard,” Suleman said.
“The Gambia simply asked that the court apply its standard to the facts that The Gambia presented, and that’s what the court did.”
The Myanmar judgement also carries implications for other genocide cases before the court, most pressingly
South Africa’s case
against Israel over its conduct in Gaza.
“The court has shown that it will carefully consider the evidence of genocide in an impartial and holistic manner," said Suleman. "I expect that it will do so in all pending and future genocide cases.”
What it means for the Rohingya
For Suleman, one of the judgment’s most important conclusions was its recognition that the Rohingya had lived in Myanmar for generations and that it was their homeland.
The court ordered Myanmar to make it possible for displaced Rohingya to return safely, voluntarily and with dignity, to reunite families and to restore property or provide replacements. It also ordered guarantees against a recurrence and compensation for the harm done.
Myanmar has two years to report on restitution and on the amount and terms of compensation. The court will decide the amount and terms in a later phase.
The judges also found that Myanmar failed to prevent genocide by people acting alongside its forces, failed to punish genocide and failed to enact legislation giving effect to the convention.
They ordered it to investigate suspects and, where warranted, prosecute and punish them.
“We’re counting on their voluntary compliance,” Jallow, the justice minister, said.
If Myanmar fails to act, he said its bilateral partners and international organisations could use the binding judgment to press it to comply.
He also pointed to the UN Charter, which allows The Gambia to turn to the Security Council if Myanmar fails to comply with the ruling. The council would decide whether to act.
Suleman said The Gambia intends to follow what Myanmar does over the next two years and press governments, the UN and regional bodies such as the OIC and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations to help secure compliance.
“My role has not ended,” he said.
“The Gambia certainly intends to continue to ensure that this judgement is fully implemented.”

items.title: Libya’s Haftar visits old foe Turkey for the first time
items.content:
Libya’s Haftar visits old foe Turkey for the first time
Submitted by
Ragip Soylu
on
Tue, 11/24/2026 - 13:27
Turkish President Erdogan is expected to host the military leader in Ankara and may seek to bring him and his rival, Libyan Prime Minister Dbeibeh, together for talks in the future
Libya's Khalifa Haftar visits Moscow military airfield on 26 September 2023 (AFP/LNA)
Off
Libyan
commander Khalifa Haftar is visiting Ankara on Tuesday, two
Turkish
sources familiar with the visit told Middle East Eye.
Reuters reported that Haftar arrived in the Turkish capital at the invitation of the Turkish government.
A Turkish source said Haftar would meet Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan during the visit.
Over the past few years, Ankara has re-established ties with Haftar, eastern Libya’s de facto ruler and commander of the Libyan Arab Armed Forces (LAAF), and has developed particularly close ties with his son Saddam.
Libya’s eastern parliament
approved
a maritime delimitation agreement with Turkey last month, marking a new chapter in relations between Ankara and eastern Libya.
Tunc Demirtas, a regional expert at the Ankara-based think tank Seta, told MEE that Turkey may soon host Libyan Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibeh, alongside Haftar, in an effort to bring the two sides closer together.
“Ankara is trying to reach its ‘One Libya’ objective, and these visits would be important to break through the deadlock,” Demirtas said.
He added that Erdogan is scheduled to visit Libya in December for the Turkey-Africa summit.
Haftar's forces execute 30 after secret military trials in eastern Libya
Read More »
Dbeibeh met Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin in Istanbul over the weekend.
Demirtas said the recent spillover from the Russia-Ukraine war into waters near Libya underscored the need for stability in and around the country.
Such stability, he said, could come only through Libya’s unification.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Monday that Ukrainian forces had sunk a
Russian
corvette and a cargo ship off Libya’s western coast.
Turkey and the
US
have been trying to broker a merger between Libya’s rival military organisations, one based in Tripoli and the other in Benghazi.
An attempt to finalise the deal last month failed after the parties could not agree on a final draft.
Turkey and other countries in the region helped mediate a US-backed agreement that representatives of Libya’s rival political camps approved in Tripoli in August.
The agreement could pave the way for presidential and legislative elections within two years.

items.title: Canadian ICC judge asks UK to release her funds frozen under US sanctions
items.content:
Canadian ICC judge asks UK to release her funds frozen under US sanctions
Submitted by
Sondos Asem
on
Tue, 11/24/2026 - 10:17
Kimberly Prost says a wedding gift and a hotel payment were blocked for months, and that she lost access to Google Maps when she needed directions in London
Judge Kimberly Prost at the headquarters of the International Criminal Court on 28 April 2026 (ICC)
Off
International Criminal Court (ICC) judge Kimberly Prost has called on Britain to act after two payments she sent to the
UK
were frozen for months under US sanctions.
Prost said she had raised the transfers with British authorities and was considering asking whether the UK’s blocking statute could help her recover the money.
The Canadian judge said one transfer was a wedding gift for a young couple and the other was a hotel payment. Both were sent from the Netherlands in euros to Britain in pounds. A US bank’s UK branch became involved in both transactions, she said.
“In the United Kingdom, I have two instances where money was blocked and remains frozen,” Prost told journalists at the court’s headquarters in The Hague.
“And this is the scenario, money sent from here in the Netherlands in euros to the United Kingdom in pounds, and I get an email which says: ‘Your money has been blocked on the basis of the order of the President of the United States, and if you want your money back, you must apply to the Office of Foreign Assets Control in the United States for a licence.’”
In response to a request for comment, the UK foreign office did not address Prost's concerns. Instead, a source said that the UK "stands with the ICC" and is opposed to the sanctions.
Her account sheds light on the personal toll of crippling US sanctions ahead of the ICC’s annual Assembly of States Parties, which opens in The Hague on 30 November.
The meeting was moved from New York over concerns that sanctions and visa restrictions would limit participation. Washington sanctioned the court itself on 9 October, after targeting individual judges and prosecutors.
'The fact that [the US is] applying these measures is futile. I like to communicate that message, because we will not be intimidated'
- Kimberly Prost, ICC judge
The meeting comes amid criticism that member states have failed to match their public support for the court with practical protection for officials such as Prost.
Washington's sanctions and threats to the ICC have been prompted by the Trump administration's opposition to the court's arrest warrant for Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the court's
Afghanistan
investigation which previously looked into US crimes.
Washington has offered member states a six-month grace period to take measures that would address US demands to amend the court's treaty to prevent the prosecution of nationals of non-member states, like the US, Russia and Israel.
Once fully in effect in April, the sanctions could stop the court from transacting in US dollars and potentially cripple its operations.
Middle East Eye revealed on Monday that Guatemala had circulated a proposal urging talks with Washington on curbing the court’s ability to pursue nationals of countries outside the ICC, echoing US and Israeli demands.
Amnesty International Secretary General Agnes Callamard accused Britain, Canada and other governments of seeking to appease Washington and called on them to act on their pledges to defend the court.
‘I have no regrets’
Washington sanctioned Prost in August 2025 over her role in a 2020 appeals ruling that authorised an investigation in Afghanistan, which could cover alleged crimes by US personnel.
Asked about a recent
decision
to close that investigation and open a separate inquiry focused on the Taliban, Prost said she had questions about the decision herself and would wait to see the outcome of the appeal lodged by the Office of the Prosecutor against the decision.
“I was sanctioned on the basis of my participation in the Appeals Chamber decision [to open the Afghanistan investigation], which I would make again today on the basis of the evidence that was in front of the Chamber,” she said. “I don’t know the state of the evidence today, only the prosecutor does. And I have no regrets about that decision whatsoever.”
Kimberly Prost, ICC judge, speaks to journalists at the court's headquarters in The Hague on 19 November 2026 (MEE/Sondos Asem)
Prost said the sanctions had left her without a credit card, made online shopping nearly impossible and stopped her from using Google Maps when she needed directions in London.
She said, however, she is undeterred and that the pressure had no bearing on her work.
“Independently and objectively, we look at the facts, the evidence, apply the law, and that’s the basis for our decision,” she said. “So the fact that they’re applying these measures is futile. I like to communicate that message, because we will not be intimidated.”
She is one of three ICC judges who have sued the Trump administration over the
sanctions
.
‘Clear red lines’
Prost said British authorities had treated the frozen transfers as a decision for private industry.
She disputed that the bank was obliged to block the funds and said she was considering asking about Britain’s blocking statute, a mechanism designed to counter certain foreign sanctions.
Exclusive: Guatemala circulates proposal to curb ICC powers in line with US-Israeli demands
Read More »
Britain was among nine countries that publicly opposed the October sanctions against the court.
“Now, in addition to those reactions and to the diplomacy, we need some strong measures being taken,” she said.
She urged governments to use legal tools to tackle overcompliance and called for more public support from civil society and judicial associations.
Prost, who helped negotiate the Rome Statute for Canada in 1998, said she supported dialogue with Washington but warned against putting the court’s jurisdiction up for negotiation. She was speaking about possible talks in general, without addressing Guatemala’s proposal specifically.
“I mean, to me, that decision to include territorial jurisdiction was at the heart of the Rome Statute, and, in addition, it’s the will of those who participated in negotiations,” she said. “You can’t just change that because a group of states decide that it’s inconvenient at this point in time.”
Under that principle, the court can pursue certain crimes committed on the territory of a member state regardless of the suspect’s nationality. Guatemala’s paper floated requiring the consent of the suspect’s country even when the alleged crimes took place in a member state.
“One thing that cannot happen is this court cannot [be made to] stop,” Prost said.

items.title: Barzani rejects Baghdad’s orders to take over Kurdish oil fields and border crossings
items.content:
Barzani rejects Baghdad’s orders to take over Kurdish oil fields and border crossings
Kurdish regional Prime Minister Masrour Barzani has called Baghdad’s move to assume authority over oil fields and border crossings in four provinces “completely unacceptable”.
“We were dismayed by the statement issued today because it goes against the talks we have held with Baghdad’s authorities,” Barzani said, according to Rudaw.
His remarks followed Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s instructions today for federal authorities to run the region’s border crossings after an investigation into oil smuggling.
Al-Zaidi tasked the Oil Ministry with overseeing Kurdish-controlled fields across four provinces and barred the Kurdistan Regional Government from authorising oil exports.
He also dismissed Kirkuk’s border crossings authority head and police chief, saying they had failed to pursue the smuggling case.

items.title: Iran says fourth tanker hits mine in Strait of Hormuz
items.content:
Iran says fourth tanker hits mine in Strait of Hormuz
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says another tanker has hit a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz, bringing the reported total to four. It said the ship took an “unauthorised” passage.
The IRGC Navy’s public relations office previously reported that mine explosions set three vessels ablaze, according to Iran’s IRNA news agency.
Strikes against ships crossing without Iranian approval have increased sharply over recent weeks as Tehran seeks to enforce its asserted control over the shipping route.

items.title: Leftwing coalition leader calls for rental revolution as Spain heads for snap election
items.content:
Exclusive: Ada Colau hopes public anger over housing will transfer into support for her Broad Front coalition in Sunday’s vote
The leader of Spain’s leftwing Broad Front coalition has called for a drastic rethink of the country’s entire housing rental system, and described the eviction of an 87-year-old woman – the spark for nationwide protests that in turn triggered Sunday’s snap general election – as “the last straw” for desperate tenants.
“We’re not interested in small changes,” Ada Colau, the former Barcelona mayor, told the Guardian in an interview. “We want to reform the entire rental sector.”

items.title: Egypt's terror list targeting European Muslims echoes Israel and the UAE
items.content:
Egypt's terror list targeting European Muslims echoes Israel and the UAE
Submitted by
Farid Hafez
on
Thu, 11/19/2026 - 17:26
Cairo has designated 35 Muslim associations across Europe as terrorists, months after an Israeli ministry report singled out many of the same names
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi (left) speaks with Luxembourg Prime Minister Luc Frieden (right) and European Council President Antonio Costa at a dinner in Brussels after the EU-Egypt summit on 22 October 2025 (Simon Wohlfahrt/Pool/AFP)
Off
In September,
Egyptian
police
arrested
all six journalists at Matsadaash, a
news platform
dedicated to fact-checking and investigative reporting. They were accused of spreading misinformation on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood, a charge the outlet denies.
The authorities then
turned
on Mada Masr, one of Egypt's best-known
independent news sites
. In October, a court ordered the site closed. The following month, its editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah, faced a
retrial
on charges of publishing false news and running an unlicensed website. The same charges brought her a one-year prison sentence in absentia in 2024.
Shaher Ayyad, an editorial board member at the news site al-Manassa,
told Reuters
: "Independent outlets are often portrayed as lawbreakers or enemies of the state."
Both cases are part of the
repression
that
Amnesty International
detailed in its 2025
report
, which found that authorities "continued to criminalize dissenting forms of expression and peaceful assembly, targeting journalists, protesters, opposition politicians and others who criticized the government's human rights record or called for political change".
Egypt's record of abuse at home has long been documented. A decade after the former military chief
took power
, the
US
State Department's 2024
human rights report
called the situation dire.
The department cited credible reports of "torture or cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment; arbitrary arrest and detention", "instances of transnational repression against individuals in another country" and "serious restrictions on freedom of expression and media freedom, including unjustified arrests or prosecutions of journalists and censorship".
The list names no organisation inside Egypt. Its targets are European institutions
On 10 November, Egypt went a step further and published a
list
of 35 associations and 36 individuals that the Cairo Criminal Court has designated as "terrorists".
Strikingly, the list names no organisation inside Egypt. Its targets are European institutions, the national, cultural, educational and religious bodies that serve
Muslim communities
across 27 countries.
At its centre is the Council of European Muslims, formerly the Federation of Islamic Organisations in Europe, an
umbrella body
founded in 1989 whose members help Muslims practise their faith, preserve their identity and integrate into their societies.
The designations are valid for five years, subject to appeal, extension and removal. They were published just days after Egyptian authorities placed the Muslim Brotherhood
permanently
on the country's terrorism list, replacing a series of time-limited designations.
For those named, the practical consequences could include restrictions on
travel and banking
, and a real threat to their
personal security
.
A European echo
Egypt's latest move has raised
fears
that it is exporting its crackdown on political dissent and extending its hunt for the Muslim Brotherhood, the movement that won the country's election in 2012 before being ousted the following year by the then defence minister, Abdel Fattah el-Sisi.
Anas Altikriti, the British-Iraqi founder of the Cordoba Foundation and one of the 36 individuals named, said Arab governments regard the political influence of Muslim communities in the West as a threat. "What you actually do is to shut down Muslim civil society in the West," he told The New Arab.
The Brotherhood bogeyman: How Europe and the US criminalise Muslim civic life
Read More »
In 2014, three years after the
Arab Spring
uprisings,
Saudi Arabia
and the
United Arab Emirates
, among others, also designated the Brotherhood a "terrorist organisation".
The list was also published a month after the European Parliament's largest group, the European People's Party,
pushed through
a
non-binding resolution
"on the need for an EU strategy to counter Islamist entryism and the influence of the Muslim Brotherhood network".
The resolution had support from fellow conservatives, the far right and liberals, and opposition from the social democrats, the Greens and the left.
It explicitly named the Council of European Muslims, along with other Muslim and
anti-racist organisations
, and
called for
groups associated with the council to be denied access to EU institutions and removed from the EU's transparency register.
Amnesty International and more than 100 other civil society groups
wrote to
European Parliament President Roberta Metsola in protest, but the letter has gone unanswered.
Given that those targeted are based in Europe, there is reason to suspect a concerted effort by political forces seeking to criminalise Muslim and anti-racist civic life. The picture, however, is bigger than that.
The global picture
It is a mistake to treat Cairo's terror list as a purely domestic decision, or even a Euro-Arab one. Egypt is better understood as part of a wider geopolitical strategy, the culmination of developments well beyond its borders.
First, Egypt has
long wanted
the Muslim Brotherhood on western terrorist lists, and some argue Sisi is acting largely on behalf of one of Egypt's main
financiers
, the UAE.
Second, it is no coincidence that those efforts gained ground under the second
Trump administration
. In November 2025, the president set in motion the
designation
of Brotherhood chapters, including Egypt's, as terrorist organisations by
executive order
rather than legislation.
That gave the Egyptian president the symbolic backing to keep telling a story that looks domestic at first glance.
The UAE, for its part,
listed
15
civil society groups
in the US and Europe as
terrorist organisations
in 2014,
alongside
armed groups such as al-Qaeda, Boko Haram and the
Islamic State
group.
They included the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the largest Muslim civil rights group in the US, and the forerunner of the Council of European Muslims, along with the national associations in
France
,
Britain
,
Germany
and Belgium that Cairo has now designated.
Muslim Brotherhood
allegations
are not a new invention, and they played a major role in November's
US midterms
, where they were levelled at Senator-elect
Abdul El-Sayed
.
In January 2025, the UAE
added
eight companies registered in the UK and owned by Emirati dissidents and their relatives.
The Israel connection
In February 2026, nine months before Egypt published its list, the
Netanyahu government's
Ministry of Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism released a
report
titled "The Muslim Brotherhood Across Europe".
The ministry makes no secret of its purpose. Its report says the ministry "systematically documents activities by those engaged in delegitimization" of Israel, and lists "cooperation with pro-Palestinian organizations" and the promotion of
boycotts, sanctions and divestment
among its areas of focus.
A match this close between an Israeli ministry's report and an Egyptian court's list is hard to dismiss as coincidence
Its research department identified nine "key organizations in Europe".
Three of them appear among the eight Europe-wide associations on the Egyptian court's list: the Council of European Muslims, the European Council for Fatwa and Research, and the European Institute of Human Sciences. The Council of European Muslims is the first organisation named in both documents.
The Israeli ministry's report presents the national associations in France, Britain, Germany and Belgium as part of the Brotherhood's European network, and all four are now on Egypt's list. Nearly a third of the 36 individuals the Egyptian court named also appear in the report, including four men it identifies as presidents of the council.
A match this close between an Israeli ministry's report and an Egyptian court's list is hard to dismiss as coincidence. It suggests Cairo is working from a script written elsewhere, further reducing the country that once led the Arab world to the role of a vessel for wealthy backers aligned with Israel.

items.title: How EU failure to regulate tech made Palestine a ‘laboratory’ for AI weaponry and surveillance
items.content:
How EU failure to regulate tech made Palestine a ‘laboratory’ for AI weaponry and surveillance
This week, the Geneva Convention
held
its Seventh Review Conference on the development of technological warfare and its humanitarian implications.
The review takes place every five years and aims to negotiate legally binding international agreements on restricting autonomous weapon systems, amid growing concerns over their use against civilians. However, powerful militarised countries like the
US
and
Russia
generally block progress.
Since the last review, the use of AI-powered weapons has accelerated exponentially, with much of the cutting-edge technology being used by
Israelis
against
Palestinians
in Gaza and the occupied West Bank by
Israel
.
Despite this, Palestine was barely mentioned during the UN
meeting
.
Last week, the Palestinian digital rights organisation
7amleh
organised a conference in Brussels, attended by Middle East Eye, bringing together policymakers, journalists, politicians and researchers to assess the use of autonomous weapons in the context of the ongoing
genocide
in Gaza.
Read more:
How EU failure to regulate tech made Palestine a ‘laboratory’ for AI weaponry and surveillance

items.content:
Nov 24 (Reuters) - Israel's Transportation Minister Miri Regev has approved the resumption of flydubai flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv pending approvals from Israeli security authorities, according to the country's transportation ministry.
Regev made the decision following a visit to the United Arab Emirates by Israeli Transportation Ministry Director General Moshe Ben Zaken, the ministry said in a statement on Monday.

items.title: Saudi air strikes kill more than 30 horses in Sanaa, Saba reports
items.content:
Saudi air strikes kill more than 30 horses in Sanaa, Saba reports
Five Saudi air strikes hit a stable in Yemen’s capital today, killing more than 30 thoroughbred horses, the Saba news agency reports.
The stable stands in Bir Zaher, within Sanaa’s Bani al-Harith district. A local source told the agency that rubble still trapped other horses.
Horses hold a prized place in Yemeni heritage as symbols of prestige and skilled horsemanship, with thoroughbreds also carrying considerable financial value.

items.title: How EU failure to regulate tech made Palestine a ‘laboratory’ for AI weaponry and surveillance
items.content:
How EU failure to regulate tech made Palestine a ‘laboratory’ for AI weaponry and surveillance
Submitted by
Fleur Hargreaves
on
Sun, 11/22/2026 - 19:03
Experts warn that spyware used by Israel on Palestinians is being exported to US and European governments for state repression at home
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar (L) addresses a press conference after a meeting at the EU headquarters on the sidelines of the EU's foreign affairs council in Brussels, 24 February 2025 (John Thys/AFP)
Off
This week, the Geneva Convention
held
its Seventh Review Conference on the development of technological warfare and its humanitarian implications.
The review takes place every five years and aims to negotiate legally binding international agreements on restricting autonomous weapon systems, amid growing concerns over their use against civilians. However, powerful militarised countries like the
US
and
Russia
generally block progress.
Since the last review, the use of AI-powered weapons has accelerated exponentially, with much of the cutting-edge technology being used by
Israelis
against
Palestinians
in Gaza and the occupied West Bank by
Israel
.
Despite this, Palestine was barely mentioned during the UN
meeting
.
Last week, the Palestinian digital rights organisation
7amleh
organised a conference in Brussels, attended by Middle East Eye, bringing together policymakers, journalists, politicians and researchers to assess the use of autonomous weapons in the context of the ongoing
genocide
in Gaza.
Nadim Nashif, 7amleh’s executive director, told the conference that Palestine is treated as a “laboratory” for AI, with technologies tested on Palestinians before being sold around the world and marketed as “battlefield-tested”.
Palestinians are among the most surveilled people on earth. Even before the genocide, he said, they were subjected to Israeli facial recognition and phone hacking, living in a “panopticon” of round-the-clock “mass surveillance”.
However, “what happened in Palestine does not stay in Palestine”, Nashif added, warning of the dangers of “having the power in the hands of a few people…controlling the future of humanity” without regulation or accountability.
Imperial boomerang
“Gaza is a trial for these technologies,” Member of European Parliament (MEP) Benedetta Scuderi told the conference.
Scuderi argued that
European defence agreements
with Israel undermine international regulations.
“When technology comes in… humanity goes away,” she said, warning that “if we lose humanity then we are done”.
Scuderi referenced the European parliament’s recent screening of Israeli film
NAZA
, a documentary compiling interviews with Israeli army officials on the uses of these technologies in Gaza.
One soldier described feeling like he was in a “video game” when using technology such as
Lavender
, Gospel and
Where’s Daddy
to locate and target Palestinians.
European countries remain complicit through their involvement in production, research and arms sales to Israel, as exemptions allow European weapons to be exported despite their use in facilitating genocide, according to
a 2025 UN report
.
Scuderi called for human rights reviews of European budgets, acknowledging that even getting such measures “on paper” is difficult, with those in power viewing them as “an extra burden”.
Without regulation, she warned, technologies developed by western governments and used by Israel against Palestinians will inevitably be deployed domestically against journalists and activists, including in her home country of Italy. This phenomenon is known as the
imperial boomerang
.
Meanwhile, EU taxpayers
continue
to fund Israeli projects. In 2025, Israeli companies, universities and research institutes received €106m from the EU’s Horizon Europe fund.
Israel's arms industry thrives on genocide and the world keeps buying
Read More »
At the conference, Harry Davies, a Guardian journalist and producer of
NAZA
, discussed a
report
he co-wrote with the documentary’s creator, Yuval Abraham, on Israel’s use of Microsoft cloud servers to store “a million calls an hour” made by Palestinians in the occupied territories.
In 2021, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella met the head of Israel’s military surveillance agency, Unit 8200, to arrange for vast amounts of data to be stored on Microsoft’s servers.
Following the investigation, Microsoft confirmed the findings and terminated its deal with the Israeli army, demonstrating the impact of journalism and public scrutiny.
While
NAZA
presents no new claims or information that Palestinians have not reported on for years, Davies said, it is “less about the actual technology than the people behind them, and the military systems” that enable the mass automated killing in Gaza.
In
response
, the Israeli army presented the technologies as mere tools, insisting decisions remain with military personnel.
The film shows “how meaningful that human involvement is”, Davies said, warning that relying on machine-generated statistical calculations can reinforce preconceived biases when operated in an atmosphere “of hatred and revenge”.
Failure of EU regulation
At the 7amleh conference, researchers from
European Digital Rights
revealed that 15 out of 27 European countries were discovered to have breached EU spyware regulations, with victims coming from civil society groups, journalists and political opponents.
In Spain, at least 65 individuals - including members of the European Parliament, Catalan presidents, legislators, jurists and members of civil society organisations - were allegedly
targeted
by the government using Pegasus spyware, developed by the Israeli firm NSO Group. The government initially denied the allegations but later acknowledged spying on 18 individuals, citing national security concerns.
'Gaza is a trial for these technologies'
- Benedetta Scuderi, Member of European Parliament
In Poland, Pegasus spyware was used to target almost
600 people
between 2017 and 2022 under the former Law and Justice government, “too many” of whom were targeted for being “inconvenient”, according to the current security services minister.
Following the scandal, the European Parliament
launched
the Pega committee in 2022 to investigate Pegasus and other spyware against civil society. However, its recommendations were never implemented.
Tech watchdog Citizen Lab
found
that a former MEP serving on the committee was hacked with Pegasus spyware at least three times during the investigation.
The European case in which an executive faced consequences was Greece’s 2022 spying scandal, known as “
Predatorgate
”, which came to light when opposition leader Nikos Androulakis discovered that his phone had been targeted with illegal spyware.
In February, a Greek court sentenced four people, including two Israelis, to prison, although an appeal remains pending.
One of the biggest obstacles to prosecution is gathering evidence, as defence and intelligence contracts are often highly classified. Another is the ability of transnational corporations to change jurisdictions to evade regulation.
Cases subsequently stall, with the EU failing to pursue them.
‘Free Europe’
In 2017, Project Maven was launched by the US to accelerate AI military intelligence, using Google as a key contractor. But following public pressure, including from its own
employees
, Google terminated the contract and formulated ethical policies.
The contract was subsequently taken over by
Palantir
, which operated Maven during the US abduction of former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and the US bombing campaign against Iran. The latter included the
“double-tap” strike
on a girls’ school in Minab, which killed more than 170 people.
Palantir also holds a contract with the Israeli army, as well as US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and is deeply
embedded
in
UK
public services, including the
National Health Service
(NHS).
In 2020, US President Donald Trump
pardoned
the CEO of Israeli company Cellebrite for assisting cybercrimes, allowing the company to subsequently secure ICE
contracts
worth up to $96m.
Serbian police and intelligence forces
used
Cellebrite technology to extract data from phones belonging to journalists and activists.
In
Russia
and
Kenya
, the software was also used to
target
political opponents of the government.
Paragon Solutions, another Israeli company that supplies phone-hacking and listening devices, saw its $2m contract with ICE
revived
by Trump after former US President Joe Biden had paused it.
Paragon spyware was used to
target
European journalists and was investigated by Italy’s parliamentary intelligence committee in 2025. The company, however, remains embedded in European markets, amid weak oversight and a reluctance to legislate and enforce regulations.
Pegasus Project: Why I was targeted by Israeli spyware
Read More »
Technologies battle-tested in Gaza are increasingly used for state repression of migrants, left-wing journalists and politicians, and the Palestine solidarity movement.
EU leaders are at a “crossroads”, MEP Cecilia Strada told the conference, arguing that they can no longer feign ignorance about their role in facilitating crimes against humanity in Gaza or the use of European technologies to profit from mass slaughter.
The European Commission will
review
the EU-Israel trade agreement after a petition calling for its full suspension surpassed 1.1 million signatures from EU citizens this week.
In 2025, the European Commission
proposed
a partial suspension of the agreement, but member states failed to adopt the measure and are unlikely to do so now.
“The relationship with Israeli companies are not the fruit of political ties… they are the infested roots of those ties,” Strada said.
She pointed to Palantir’s lucrative UK contracts, describing them as not only “a threat to our democracies and fundamental rights, but also a fraud”, diverting public money away from public services and into private profit.
After visiting Palestine, Strada said she had witnessed the realities of systematic surveillance and brutality, and began to see parallels in the use of the same technologies in Europe.
“Our role is not to free Palestine, but to free Europe,” she said, so it will be “not us which saved Palestinians, but Palestinians that saved us… from a dark future”.

items.title: Israel kills UN worker and two others across Gaza as attacks on Palestinians continue
items.content:
Israel kills UN worker and two others across Gaza as attacks on Palestinians continue
Submitted by
Alex MacDonald
on
Tue, 11/24/2026 - 10:23
At least 1,679 Palestinians have been killed since a 'ceasefire' was agreed in October 2025
A member of the Palestinian civil defence douses the flames on a car that was targeted in an Israeli strike in Gaza City on 23 November (AFP/Omar al-Qattaa)
Off
Israeli
strikes across Gaza have killed three
Palestinians
, including a worker for the United Nations agency for Palestine refugees (Unrwa).
The organisation on Monday named the staff member who was killed as Adel al-Helo, who had been working near a well in the Jabalia refugee camp in the north of the enclave when killed.
Reuters reported another Israeli air strike ⁠targeting a vehicle in western Gaza City, killing two people and wounding others.
In a statement, Unrwa called for the protection of humanitarian workers following the killing.
Unrwa said its Commissioner-General ad interim Christian Saunders was "greatly saddened" by the killing of the agency's staff member alongside the wounding of three others.
"They were carrying out their regular duties at a water well, providing critical services to the community," the agency said in a post on X. "Humanitarian workers must be protected at all times."
A total of 397 Unrwa personnel and its partners have been killed since Israel began its genocide in the besieged territory.
"Gaza is the deadliest place for UN aid workers since the United Nations was created in the wake of World War II. This must and cannot be normalised. There must be an independent investigation and accountability," the agency added.
Meningitus outbreak
The killings mark the latest Israeli violations of a US-negotiated "ceasefire" that began in October 2025.
At least 1,679 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since the "ceasefire" was agreed, continuing the ongoing genocide in the enclave.
Israel likely to lose Gaza genocide case if ICJ follows Myanmar ruling, Tel Aviv scholar says
Read More »
On Tuesday, Gaza’s health ministry issued an “epidemiological alert” across the territory, warning that a “shocking” increase in meningitis infections puts hundreds of thousands of lives at risk, particularly children.
The ministry urged the World Health Organization and Unicef to launch an emergency response.
Nidal Ghunaim, deputy director general of primary healthcare for public health, reported 272 cases in October. He described the figure as more than eight times the usual monthly average of 30 to 50.
Meningitis has killed 15 people this year, Ghunaim said, including five during the August-to-October surge.
The ministry described the outbreak as an “inevitable result of the destruction of infrastructure, overcrowding of shelters, mixing of drinking water with sewage, and the disaster being exacerbated by flooding due to rain”.
“We hold the [Israeli] occupation fully and directly responsible for the epidemic outbreak due to its prevention of the entry of maintenance spare parts, sterilization materials and fuel,” it said.

items.title: US envoy 'not certain' military aid to Israel will end this year as Trump promised
items.content:
By Alexander Cornwell
TEL AVIV, Nov 24 (Reuters) - US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee has cast doubt on whether Washington would end its $3.8 billion in annual military aid to Israel by the end of this year, as promised by President Donald Trump on the day of this month's midterm elections.
In his surprise announcement as voters headed to the polls on November 3, Trump said he had made a deal with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu several months earlier to stop providing Israel with around $4 billion in annual US funding.

items.title: Saudi strikes on Yemen buses and trucks leave 25 dead or missing: Report
items.content:
Saudi strikes on Yemen buses and trucks leave 25 dead or missing: Report
Saudi aircraft struck buses and trucks in Wadi Maabaq in Yemen’s Lahj governorate, leaving 25 people dead or missing and wounding six, the Saba news agency reports.
Residents told Saba that badly burnt remains were still inside one of two buses hit in the attack, hampering identification.
They said Saudi warplanes continued circling overhead, blocking ambulance crews and residents from reaching those caught in the strikes and worsening the toll.
This screen grab taken from video footage released by Ansarullah Media Centre on November 23, 2026, shows Images of the aftermath of a Saudi strike on buses and trucks in Wadi Mabaq, Lahj governorate, southwestern Yemen. An airstrike on trucks and buses killed 26 people in Yemen's southwest, local officials told AFP on November 24, 2026, as the Houthis and government forces traded blame for the attack. Yemen, one of the world's poorest countries, has become the most active front in the Middle East war with the Iran-backed Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition exchanging frequent attacks.

Before departure, medics provided care at the al-Mawasi field hospital. The Red Crescent arranged the evacuation with the World Health Organization, according to the Palestinian news agency.
Local medical sources say injuries among Palestinians have exceeded 6,000 since the so-called “ceasefire” began in Gaza.

Meningitis has killed 15 people this year, Ghunaim said, including five during the August-to-October surge.
The ministry described the outbreak as an “inevitable result of the destruction of infrastructure, overcrowding of shelters, mixing of drinking water with sewage, and the disaster being exacerbated by flooding due to rain”.
“We hold the [Israeli] occupation fully and directly responsible for the epidemic outbreak due to its prevention of the entry of maintenance spare parts, sterilization materials and fuel,” it said.

items.title: Israel kills senior Hamas security official in airstrike on Gaza
items.content:
By Nidal al-Mughrabi
CAIRO, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Israel killed a senior Hamas security official in an airstrike on Gaza on Tuesday which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said showed there was no escape from his country's "long reach."
Naeem Abu Nahel, the director of Hamas' internal security apparatus in Gaza, was one of at least seven Palestinians killed in the Gaza Strip, including two police officers, Palestinian medics and police said.

items.content:

A leader of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has said he was prevented from leaving Delhi to fly to the UK to give talks on the viral group’s protests.
Saurav Das, 27, has been at the forefront of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), which has amassed millions of social media followers
since its launch in May
. Das, who was due to fly out early on Tuesday, said immigration officials told him at the airport that his passport had been flagged.

items.title: After 80 years in Oxford, Naga ancestors are finally going home
items.content:
A campaign securing the landmark return to India of ancestral remains taken during British colonial rule has opened a wider conversation about restitution
The lacerating legacy of colonialism survives in many spaces, particularly in museum collections and private holdings across the western world. And it’s not just limited to inanimate artefacts or cultural objects.
For almost 80 years, human remains were displayed on crowded glass shelves at
Pitt Rivers Museum
at Oxford University, one of the world’s most celebrated institutions.

items.content: قال الرئيس الأميركي دونالد ترامب إنه يتوقع أن تشتري شركات الطيران الصينية 250 طائرة إضافية من شركة صناعة الطائرات الأميركية بوينغ، في أحدث تطور في حملة المبيعات المستمرة التي يقوم بها الرئيس الأميركي لفتح ثاني أكبر سوق للطيران في العالم أمام شركة الطائرات الأميركية لأول مرة منذ حوالي عشر سنوات.

items.title: جيش العدو الصهيوني يعلن عن إحصائية جديدة
items.content:
جيش العدو الصهيوني يعلن عن إحصائية جديدة

- يقدم القسم حالياً الدعم لـ 92,300 جريح وجريحة من مختلف الحروب التي خاضتها "إسرائيل".
- نحو ثلث العدد (31,500 شخص) أصيبوا خلال الحرب الأخيرة.
- يعاني 43,800 شخص (أي 47%) من إصابات نفسية واضطراب ما بعد الصدمة، منهم 19,600 أصيبوا في الحرب الأخيرة.
- تعرض نحو 1,100 شخص لبتر في الأطراف.
- يعاني 123 جريح من فقدان البصر.
- صُنِّف 602 شخص ضمن فئة ذوي أعلى درجات الإعاقة.
- يعاني 3900 جريح من إصابات في الرأس متفاوتة الشدة، من بينهم 249 شخصاً يواجهون إصابات معقدة في الرأس.
- من بين جميع الجرحى، يعيش 602 شخصاً في أشد مستويات الإعاقة، والتي تُصنف ضمن فئة "الإعاقة الخاصة" بنسبة 100%.

items.title: Malaysia to send thousands of migrants back to Myanmar as PM acknowledges junta’s ‘atrocities’
items.content:
Prime minister Anwar Ibrahim’s announcement comes days after the ICJ found Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya minority
Malaysia says it will send thousands of migrants and refugees back to Myanmar, despite acknowledging that many asylum seekers in the country had been victims of “atrocities” carried ​out by the junta in Naypyidaw.
The announcement comes just days after the UN’s highest court ruled Myanmar had committed genocide against its Rohingya minority.

Ebikes, screens and failing manners pose challenge for Dutch cycling culture
items.content:
Awareness campaign reminds public ‘traffic is a team sport’ amid less civility and more collisions on roads
For decades the Netherlands has been famed for its proud cycling culture, with a network of 23,000 miles of bike paths used by everyone from children under eight to adults over 80.
In recent years, however, like so many countries around the world, it has seen a dramatic change in the type of vehicles using those lanes: no longer the preserve of pedal bikes, they are used by all manner of two-wheeled vehicles including electric cargo bikes, thick-tyred “fatbikes”, speed pedelecs, electric scooters and even some micro cars.
